headings.text: How it fits into the platform

blocks.html:
This page orients developers and operators on what the MediaMTX integration is in the OpenDefence context: what the streaming server does, what the integration API adds, and how the product plugs into the Deploy App core. It is deliberately short — the runtime detail lives in the MediaMTX stack (Kubernetes) page, which describes the closed-alpha opendefence-platform and is provisional.

What MediaMTX does here

The streaming server itself is upstream MediaMTX (bluenviron/mediamtx), an off-the-shelf single-binary media server. In an OpenDefence deployment it is the live-video product: field units publish streams — a drone feed, a phone camera — over RTMPS, RTSPS or SRT, and anyone who needs the picture views them over HLS (low-latency variant) or WebRTC in a plain browser. Plaintext RTSP and RTMP are switched off (rtspEncryption/rtmpEncryption: "strict" in mediamtx.yml), so those transports are TLS-only; SRT carries its own optional encryption.

What vanilla MediaMTX lacks is any notion of who is streaming. The OpenDefence integration closes that gap: MediaMTX runs with authMethod: http, so every publish and every read triggers an authorization callback to the integration API (/api/v1/mediamtx/auth) before any media flows. The credentials being checked are provisioned per enrolled user, so stream access follows the same callsign identity that gates everything else in Deploy App. The essence in one picture:

blocks.html:
The integration API: mtxrmapi

mtxrmapi (image ghcr.io/pvarki/mediamtx-integration, listening on port 8005) is the piece that connects MediaMTX to the Deploy App core. It runs as a sidecar-style container in the same pod as the mediamtx server and plays three roles:

  • Product API for the core — it implements the integration contract that rmapi calls to initialize the product and provision users as they are added or revoked, plus the standard /api/v1/healthcheck. Its state lives in its own database (CNPG cluster mtx-postgres).
  • Auth backend for MediaMTX — it answers the per-connection /api/v1/mediamtx/auth callbacks described above, deciding each publish/read against the credentials it manages.
  • Product UI — it ships the MTX web UI files (connection details, per-user credentials), which a companion nginx container serves to enrolled users under /ui/mtx on the mTLS host.

Its configuration uses the RMMTX_ environment prefix; notably RMMTX_RMCN pins the service-mesh identity of rmapi, so the integration only accepts core calls from the real core.

How it fits into the platform

MediaMTX is registered as product mtx in the core's kraftwerk registry (kraftwerk-rasenmaeher-init.json), which tells rmapi to reach it at mtx-server-internal.app-mtx.svc.cluster.local:8005 and which Linkerd certificate CN to expect from it. The product mounts its own kraftwerk-init.json pointing back at rmapi, so the hub-and-spoke wiring is mutually authenticated. The full pattern — shared by TAK and Matrix — is described in Integration pattern.

Per-user access rides the callsign identity: users enroll through the core, rmapi mints them a client certificate whose CN is their callsign, and behind that mTLS gate they pick up the personal streaming credentials that mtxrmapi issued for the same callsign. How the core issues and validates those identities is covered in Core services. The raw streaming ports themselves bypass the HTTP edge entirely — how that works, port by port, is the stack page's job.

Where to go next

  • Using MediaMTX as an end user (getting your stream credentials, publishing from an app, watching a feed): see the MTX Guide book on the Guides shelf of this site.
  • How it actually runs — pod layout, exposed ports, TLS material, database, honest rough edges: MediaMTX stack (Kubernetes). Remember that page describes the closed-alpha Kubernetes platform.
  • Building something like this for your own product: the MediaMTX integration is a good model of a mid-complexity integration — start at the integration overview.
